title: Electrochemical reduction of CO2 on electrodeposited Cu electrodes crystalline phase sensitivity on selectivity
abstract: The product distribution of electrochemical reduction of CO2 can be altered by modifying the surface of pure copper by deposition. In this study, chronoamperometric deposition of Cu on Cu (Cu/Cu) was carried out at two different CuSO4 bath concentrations, 0.25 M (high) and 0.025 M (low), termed as Cu/Cu-H and Cu/Cu-L respectively. These deposits were characterized by X-ray diffraction and they vary in their crystal orientation. Pure Cu and Cu/Cu were aligned towards (1 1 1) and (2 2 0) plane with a texture coefficient of 1.2 and 1.7, respectively. Electrodeposited electrodes were tested for the electrochemical reduction of CO2 in KCl electrolyte and the results were compared with that of pure Cu electrode. Electrochemical reduction opper lectrodeposition exture coefficient ethane of CO2 showed methane and ethane, with hydrogen as the byproduct. The product distribution varied with the crystal orientation of Cu electrodes. The maximum Faradaic efficiency of methane was 26% obtained on pure Cu electrode with (1 1 1) and (2 0 0) orientation, whereas Cu/Cu-L with dominating (2 2 0) orientation showed a maximum formation of ethane with Faradaic efficiency of 43%. A possible mechanism of product formation on Cu towards C1 and Cu/Cu towards C2 is also discussed. © 2014 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved.

. Introduction
Fossil fuels based anthropogenic emission of CO2 can be counered by utilizing enormous CO2 as carbon source in all possible ays [1,2]. As of now, excess of 3.9% of CO2 is added to the carbon ycle every year [3]. The innovative process of CO2 utilization needs o be energy independent. Hence, adopting any kind of renewable nergy based chemical conversion process such as photochemical, lectrochemical and solar-thermal processes which can both actiate CO2 and produce chemicals are in need [4]. Among which, the lectrochemical based reduction of CO2 forms desired intermedites, offers potential for industrial applicability [5].
The product formed on electrochemically reducing CO2 depends n nature of electrode material and of the solvent including cations nd anions, local pH, electrolyte and CO2 pressure [6,7]. Considring metallic electrode for CO2 reduction, metals with medium ydrogen overvoltage characteristics are unique, since they prouce hydrocarbons in significant amounts [8]. Literature reports hat Cu, belonging to the medium hydrogen overvoltage metal as extensively studied and still offers potential on its surface

[10] used polypyrrole coated Cu catalyst for reducing the overpotential of CO2 reduction. The studies focus on modification of copper rather than screening other metals towards CO2 reduction [11].
Fine-tuning of Cu electrode composition will enhance the performance for reduction of CO2. For instance, the surface area of the copper was made to increase by ex-situ deposition of Cu on Cu electrodes and the effect of surface morphology was studied on CO2 reduction by Goncalves et al. [11]. Tang et al. found that a Cu electrode covered with Cu nanoparticles exhibits higher selectivity towards hydrocarbons due to a greater abundance of under-coordinated sites [12]. Next to electrode, the selection of electrolyte plays a role in product distribution [6,7]. The property of electrolyte should be based on its CO2 solubility, buffering capacity and also on the mode of adsorption of cations and anions in the inner Helmholtz plane. Recently, a report on modified Cu electrode shows the variation of hydrocarbon (C1/C2) ratio in bicarbonate electrolyte [11], but no such investigation on halide electrolyte was reported. Xadsorbed–C bond in halide electrolyte provides good platform to study CO2 reduction on modified Cu surfaces [13].

. Experimental
.1. Pretreatment
Commercially available Cu sheets purchased from Alfa Aesar ere cut in to 1 cm2 strips. The sheets were polished with 220 esh emery paper for a minute, and washed with acetone and
istilled water. The etching on pretreated copper foil was carried ut at a potential of 2.3 V between two Cu electrodes for 2 min in .5 M H3PO4 [14]. During etching, the impurities were eliminated nd the effect of such concentrated electrolyte alters the surface orphology and thus leaves a number of low coordinated sites 12,15,16].
.2. Electrodeposition of Cu on Cu
Constant voltage technique was employed for depositing Cu at 0.3 V (vs. Ag/AgCl) for 5 min in a three electrode setup containing retreated Cu as the working electrode and Pt as counter electrode. he electrolytic bath consists of 0.25 M and 0.025 M CuSO4 solution ith pH adjusted to 1 with H2SO4 [17]. The weight % of Cu deposited rom 0.25 M and 0.025 M CuSO4 solution was 1.58% and 0.158% with espect to the base copper, respectively. Deposition was repeated or uniformity and characterized by SEM and XRD.
.3. Catalyst characterization
.3.1. X-ray diffraction The XRD patterns of the deposited electrodes were obtained ith high resolution X-ray diffractometer (PAN analytical X’pert RO), using Cu K radiation at 45 kV and 20 mA. The scan rate was .04◦ min−1 in the range 2 = 10–90◦.
.3.2. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM)
The images were obtained using a Hitachi Scanning Electron icroscope (S4800 FESEM), equipped with an energy dispersive nalytical system (EDS, EDAX HORIBA).
2.4. Electroreduction of CO2
All the electrochemical experiments were carried out in an Htype cell separated by a glass frit. An Ag/AgCl (3.5 M saturated KCl) and Pt foil were used as reference and counter electrodes, respectively. All experiments were carried out in room temperature (23 ± 1 ◦C). The electrochemical measurements were performed in EC epsilon potentiostat in aqueous KCl solution saturated with CO2. The pH change was monitoring during the course of the reaction using a pH/Ion meter (Eutech). The potentials reported are expressed with respect to reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) incorporating the pH of the solution as reported by Kuhl et al. using the formula: V vs. (RHE) = V measured vs. (Ag/AgCl) + 0.197 + (0.0598 × pH of the solution) [18].
2.5. Product analysis
Gaseous products obtained during the electroreduction were analyzed at regular intervals manually by gas chromatography (GCPerkin-Elmer Clarus 800) equipped with Poraplot Q column and Molecular sieve column. The FID detector with N2 as carrier gas was used to analyze the hydrocarbons and the TCD detector with the same carrier gas was used for permanent gas analysis. The liquid phase products were analyzed by GC, HPLC (with Chromotopak C-18 column using UV detector) and also by titrimetric analysis, but, no significant products were observed. The estimated limit of detection for formic acid in HPLC is 2 ppb. Hence, we accounted only for the gaseous products, considering liquid phase products below the detectable limits.

3.1. Catalyst characterization
Chronoamperometry was used as an electrochemical method for copper deposition, and simultaneously, as a technique suitable for electrochemical nucleation studies. In this study, the potential was −0.3 V (vs. Ag/AgCl) [17] which was near the equilibrium potential of Cu/Cu (II) ions and two different concentrations of 0.25 M and 0.025 M of CuSO4 were employed for deposition. Enhancement in CO2 reduction by the addition of steps and inks to atomically flat Cu surface has been reported by Hori et al. 25], and Takahashi et al. [27] reported higher yield of C2 when n = 2 n (1 1 0) plane due to the presence of two neighboring step lines. In ddition, as reported by Hori et al., when a cyrstal surface of (2 2 0) lane has step lines adjacent to (1 1 1) plane, it suppresses the foration of methane and promotes the formation of the intermediate pecies though C–C bonding [25]. Previous reports have shown that electrolyte choice has proound effect on Faradaic efficiency and product selectivity for he reduction of CO2 on Cu electrodes [28], and the mechanistic spect is governed by the anion and cation of the electrolyte [29]. iterature reports that the conversion efficiency decreases in the rder of K+ » Li+ > Na+ for cation and Cl− » HSO4− >HCO3− > NO3− or anion [30]. We also performed a comparative study of CO2
reduction in KCl and KHCO3 electrolytes for the electrodeposited Cu electrodes where the pH change and products obtained were monitored. Fig. 8 compares the products formed on Cu/Cu-H in KCl and KHCO3 electrolyte at −1.0 V vs. RHE. As can be seen from the Figure, methane, ethane and hydrogen were the major products observed in both the electrolytes. The Faradaic efficiency of ethane in KCl (18%) is higher than KHCO3 (5%), while the Faradaic efficiency of methane in KCl (6%) is slightly lower than KHCO3 (9%). However, no significant difference in Faradaic efficiency for hydrogen evolution was observed for KCl (60%) and KHCO3 (57%).
The pH of solution saturated with N2 and CO2 for KCl and KHCO3 is shown in Table 2 for the electrodeposited Cu/Cu-H as a representative system. For KCl solution, the pH of the working electrode compartment was 3.3 at the start of the electrolysis (after CO2 purging), which increased to 12.0 after electrolysis, while the pH of the counter electrode compartment remained acidic throughout the electrolysis; it changes from 5.2 (before electrolysis) to 2.0 at the end of electrolysis. nd KHCO3 arises because KHCO3 has a neutralizing capacity for ydroxide ions generated by the reduction reactions, while KCl has ot. However, the hydrogen evolution was similar for both the elecrolytes, and further studies are required to correlate the pH change o the product obtained.
In KCl electrolyte, Cl− ions suppress the adsorption of protons romoting C–C reaction [13], and the solvated potassium ions and hloride ions helps in activating CO2. The Cl− ion adsorption stabiizes intermediates and reduces the overpotential required for the ormation of first intermediate •CO2− in the CO2 reduction reaction 31]. Moreover, in KCl solution, as the potential is applied, the elecrons are transferred from the chloride ion to the vacant orbital of O2, to form CO as intermediate. CO on protonation/electronation teps forms a •CH2 group which on further dimerization and proonation can form ethane [32] or it can stabilize as methane based n the altered surface morphology of the deposit. These results ndicate that production of C2 is favored on a roughened surface, referably with aligned (2 2 0) planes.
. Conclusion
The electrochemical reduction of CO2 was performed on lectrodeposited Cu electrodes in KCl electrolyte. The product foration was observed by varying the reduction potential and the esults are compared with that of pure Cu electrode. The maxium Faradaic efficiency of methane was 26% on Cu electrode in omparison to 20% on electrodeposited Cu. Whereas, the maxium Faradaic efficiency of ethane was 43% on electrodeposited u/Cu in comparison to Faradaic efficiency of 10% on bare Cu. he reason could be due to the alignment of expressed plane hich was identified by the calculation of the texture coeffiient. Pure Cu was oriented towards (1 1 1) and (2 0 0) planes, n contrast to electrodeposited Cu which was oriented towards 2 2 0) plane. Thus, Cu favors methane formation and electrodeosited Cu/Cu favors ethane formation in the presence of KCl lectrolyte.
